```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(orchestraManifest)
```

## Why a typed result at all

A collection of analytics components becomes a framework only when one
component's output is another's input by construction. The alternative is
what most multi-package stacks actually do -- each component returns its own
list or data frame, and every pairing needs a bespoke adapter written by
whoever wired it, checked by nobody, and silently wrong the day either side
changes shape.

The manifest is the single result type that removes those adapters. An
emitter fills it in once and every consumer reads the same properties in the
same places, whatever produced them. Three properties of the type do the real
work.

It is **versioned**, so a consumer can say which schema it understands and
refuse anything else. It is **hashed**, so a consumer can tell whether the
payload it is holding is the payload the emitter sealed. And it is
**provenance-tracked**, so an approximation cannot quietly lose the identity
of the thing it approximated.

## The class

```{r class}
params <- data.frame(a = c(0.12, 0.15), b = c(1.51, 1.44))

m <- orchestra_manifest(
  emitter_package    = "example",
  emitter_version    = "0.1.0",
  inferential_target = "parameters",
  run_id             = "example-001",
  method             = "example:demo",
  seed               = 7L,
  params             = params,
  timestamp          = as.POSIXct("2026-07-05 09:00:00", tz = "UTC"),
  data_hash          = manifest_data_hash(params, NULL, NULL, NULL, 7L)
)

m@emitter_package
m@manifest_version
```

The properties fall into four groups. Identity says what this is and what made
it. Semantics says what it is about, drawn from a closed vocabulary a consumer
can dispatch on before it inspects any payload.

```{r targets}
inferential_targets()
```

Payload carries the load-bearing content -- `params`, `outputs`, `weights`,
`obs_target`, `summary` and `seed` -- and is exactly the set the hash covers.
Provenance records what the result was derived from.

## Emit, verify, consume

The hash is taken over the payload only. Schema version, emitter identity and
timestamp are metadata, so re-tagging a manifest leaves an unchanged payload
verifying, while any edit to the payload is caught.

```{r verify}
verify_manifest(m)$ok

m@emitter_package <- "relabelled"
verify_manifest(m)$ok
```

Tampering with the payload is a different matter.

```{r tamper}
tampered <- m
tampered@params$a[1] <- 0.99

verify_manifest(tampered)
```

`verify_manifest()` returns its verdict as data because a consumer often wants
to record a failure and carry on with the other lenses it has. The loud
version is `consume_manifest()`, which is what a gate should call. It runs
three checks -- is this a manifest, is its schema one I accept, does its
payload still verify -- and errors on any of them.

```{r consume, error = TRUE}
consume_manifest(m)@run_id

consume_manifest(tampered)
```

The version check is the one that earns its keep. Coercing silently across a
schema boundary is how a pipeline ends up reading a slot that no longer means
what it meant when the consumer was written, and the failure surfaces far
downstream as a wrong number rather than as an error.

```{r version, error = TRUE}
consume_manifest(m, accept = "1.0.0")
```

## Provenance is not optional for a derived result

A manifest that approximates another one records a compact handle to it. The
handle carries the upstream `data_hash`, not just its `run_id`, so a later
re-emission that changed the numbers cannot be passed off as the same input.

```{r lineage}
manifest_lineage(m)
```

Setting `metadata$derived` to `TRUE` turns the lineage from a convention into
a rule the class validator enforces.

```{r derived, error = TRUE}
orchestra_manifest(
  emitter_package    = "proxy",
  emitter_version    = "0.1.0",
  inferential_target = "parameters",
  run_id             = "proxy-001",
  method             = "proxy:demo",
  metadata           = list(derived = TRUE),
  timestamp          = Sys.time(),
  data_hash          = manifest_data_hash(data.frame(), NULL, NULL, NULL,
                                          NA_integer_)
)
```

## A verdict is not an ensemble

A causal test or a decision produces one labelled conclusion, not a matrix of
draws. Forcing it into `params` as a single-row table leaves a consumer unable
to tell a verdict from a degenerate posterior, so it gets a typed home of its
own in `summary`. Because `summary` is inside the hash, a tampered verdict is
detected exactly like a tampered payload.

```{r summary}
verdict <- manifest_summary(
  "insufficient evidence",
  abstained = TRUE,
  abstain_reason = "effective sample size below the floor",
  metrics = list(ess = 41)
)

verdict$abstained
verdict$abstain_reason
```

## Refusals and abstentions

An abstention is a result, not a failure. A component that will not stand
behind a number should say so in a way a gate can recognise, and the problem
is that recognition used to depend on knowing which component produced it.
More than one component exports a predicate named `is_refusal()`, each
recognises only its own class, and when two are attached the bare name
resolves to whichever was attached last -- returning `FALSE` on the other
component's genuine refusal. That is a silent false negative, and a gate that
should have stopped sails straight through it.

The contract fixes this with a naming convention plus a pair of
producer-agnostic predicates. A structured refusal has a class ending in
`_refusal` and a structured abstention a class ending in `_abstention`, which
holds across object systems because the class vector of an S3 refusal and of
an S7 one both end that way.

```{r refusal}
s3_refusal <- structure(list(why = "no data"), class = "example_refusal")
s7_refusal <- structure(list(),
                        class = c("example::example_refusal", "S7_object"))
abstention <- structure(list(), class = "example_abstention")

c(is_orchestra_refusal(s3_refusal), is_orchestra_refusal(s7_refusal))
```

Gate logic almost always wants the wider union, because a refusal and an
abstention mean the same thing to a gate.

```{r decline}
vapply(list(s3_refusal, s7_refusal, abstention, 42),
       is_orchestra_decline, logical(1))
```

Seam-side code that mints a refusal of its own has no component name to follow
the convention with, so it stamps the explicit marker instead. The stamp is
idempotent, and a refusal can therefore pass through several layers without
accumulating duplicate classes.

```{r marker}
r <- as_orchestra_refusal(structure(list(why = "capital firewall"),
                                    class = "list"))
class(r)
identical(as_orchestra_refusal(r), r)
```

## Grounding tokens

The grounding vocabulary is orthogonal to the refusal contract: a token says
how well a fact is evidenced, a refusal says what happened to the control
flow. A fact is grounded only when its verification date is present.

```{r tokens}
grounding_token(as.Date(c("2026-07-05", "2026-07-06")))
grounding_token(as.Date(c("2026-07-05", NA)))
grounding_token(as.Date(character(0)))
```

The asymmetry is the point. An empty evidence set is not neutral, it is the
absence of evidence, and a partially checked set is not partially trustworthy
because the consumer cannot tell which element it may lean on. Both collapse
to `[unverified]` so a downstream gate errs towards abstention. Combining
tokens follows the same rule, worst-case across the inputs.

```{r combine}
combine_grounding(c(GROUNDING_GROUNDED, GROUNDING_GROUNDED))
combine_grounding(c(GROUNDING_GROUNDED, GROUNDING_UNVERIFIED))
```

Any other rule -- a majority, a mean, an optimistic "at least one" -- would
let a verdict inherit confidence from its checked inputs while quietly resting
on an unchecked one.

## Comparing two manifests honestly

A purely structural conformance check cannot catch a wrong-but-agreed
convention. Two components that both label a column `o1` will compare happily
even when one means tonnes per hectare and the other kilograms per hectare,
and the resulting number is wrong by a factor nobody downstream can recover.

The guard compares the semantic descriptors rather than the column positions,
and refuses on a disagreement.

```{r schema, error = TRUE}
with_unit <- function(unit, run_id) {
  orchestra_manifest(
    emitter_package    = "example",
    emitter_version    = "0.1.0",
    inferential_target = "predictions",
    run_id             = run_id,
    method             = "example:demo",
    obs_schema = list(outputs = data.frame(name = c("o1", "o2"),
                                           quantity = "grain_yield",
                                           unit = c(unit, "t/ha"))),
    timestamp          = Sys.time(),
    data_hash = manifest_data_hash(data.frame(), NULL, NULL, NULL,
                                   NA_integer_)
  )
}

assert_obs_schema_correspondence(with_unit("t/ha", "a"),
                                 with_unit("t/ha", "b"))

assert_obs_schema_correspondence(with_unit("t/ha", "a"),
                                 with_unit("kg/ha", "b"))
```

The check is opt-in by presence: when either manifest lacks an `obs_schema` it
is a graceful no-op, so the guard activates once both emitters populate the
field and no existing pipeline breaks on the day it lands.

## Adapting a component

A component joins the contract by being adapted, not by being rewritten. It
keeps its own result type and a method on `as_orchestra_manifest()` lifts that
type into a manifest. Two adapters ship here, for a `PESTO` ensemble manifest
and a `proxymix` mixture fit, and each is registered at load time only when
its component is installed.

```{r adapter, eval = requireNamespace("proxymix", quietly = TRUE)}
set.seed(1)
draws <- matrix(stats::rnorm(200), 100, 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("a", "b")))
fit <- proxymix::fit_proxymix(proxymix::gmm_target_from_samples(draws),
                              N = 2L, regime = "sample", max_iter = 50L)

proxy <- manifest_from_gmm(fit, seed = 1L, consumed = list(m))

proxy@emitter_package
proxy@metadata$derived
proxy@consumed_manifests[[1]]$run_id
verify_manifest(proxy)$ok
```

## Two class identities, one contract

The contract was a script sourced into a coordination workspace before it was
a package. A manifest minted by that reference carries the bare class name,
one minted here carries the package-qualified name, and a component that
implements the contract without depending on this package mints the bare form
too.

```{r identity}
class(m)
is_orchestra_manifest(m)
```

They are the same contract, so identity is tested on the class name -- the
part the contract actually fixes -- rather than with a strict class check that
would reject every manifest emitted anywhere else. The package's test suite
includes a cross-implementation oracle for exactly this: it builds a manifest
under the reference implementation in a separate R session, hashes the same
payload under both implementations, and requires the two strings to be
identical. An extraction that quietly changed the digest would pass every
self-consistent test in the suite and fail that one.
